newsitem.title: UK: Oil sees mild recovery but traders see more falls.
newsitem.headline: Oil sees mild recovery but traders see more falls.

text.p: World oil prices firmed slightly on Monday in a technical recovery after last week's headlong slide, but dealers said the market still looked vulnerable.

London March futures for benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude oil last traded 16 cents firmer at $21.11 a barrel in what traders predicted would turn out to be a short-term correction to a fundamentally weaker market.

Brent fell more than $1.50 last week as demand for winter heating oil faded, putting paid to a rally which took crude to a six-year high of $25 in mid-October and kept prices high to the middle of January.
Brent on Friday fell below $21 a barrel for the first time since last August and for much of Monday again traded under $21.
"It's not looking good," said analyst Steve Kwan at MMS International. "The break of $21 a barrel per barrel has really set the tone for further moves to the downside."
Dealers said the fall in demand for heating oil had not yet been replaced by spring gasoline buying.
"We're in the in-between season," said analyst Bill O'Grady at A.G. Edwards in the United States. "It's too early for gasoline to help the market and it's too late for heating oil."
Dealers said that, despite strong demand patterns, rising inventories of crude had undercut crude prices just as refiners had cut operations for seasonal repairs.

Forecasts are that extra supplies of crude from a range of non-OPEC producers, as well as a gradual rise from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) itself, will prove more than a match for fast-rising world demand in the months to come.

The West's energy watchdog, the International Energy Agency (IEA), said on Friday that it expected supplies of crude from producers outside of OPEC to rise a huge two million bpd this year. It saw demand going up 1.9 million bpd.

Distillate stocks, including heating oil and diesel, in the leading industrial nations ended last year 12 million barrels higher than a year earlier, in surplus for the first time in 19 months, the IEA said.
